name: Karl Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good afternoon, Karl, and thanks for the tea. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at five, prayers, then out. We've got a hundred and eighty acres that my grandfather bought in 1951, a herd of sixty Hereford cattle and about two hundred ewes. My son Daniel works with me, he's thirty-two, and he'll have it when I'm done. We do the stock in the morning, and in summer it's hay, proper meadow hay, cut and turned and baled ourselves. Margaret keeps the books in a ledger at the kitchen table, same as my mother did.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like working with my son. My father and I worked these same fields, and now it's Daniel and me. What wears me out is the government. Every year there's a new scheme, a new rule, and a new form to fill in on a website that doesn't work. I've never touched one of those AI things and I don't intend to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, after chapel on Sunday, over the tea urn. Folk round here never believed the half of it. I'd say good honest work wins in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thankful, and I'd mean that in the church sense. My grandfather bought this land with sweat, and I'd like to hand it to Daniel the same way, not with a computer in the middle. That's all I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as now. We'd buy the bit of rough ground off the Pritchards when old Owen retires, if the price is fair, maybe sixty thousand from savings. Daniel and I would do the hay as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad. Like a good harvest in the barn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change on the farm in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: New gates on the top field, they're older than Daniel. That's about it. You don't change what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Daniel feel the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's a bit more modern than me, he's got the phone with the maps on it. He'd probably want one of those cameras to watch the calving shed. I'd let him, if he pays for it.

S0.say: I told you so, and folk round here never believed the half of it. Good honest work wins in the end.
S0.think: I'd be thankful. My grandfather bought this land with sweat, and I'd like to hand it to Daniel the same way, without a computer in the middle.
S0.do: Carries on exactly as now with the cattle, sheep and hay. Buys a neighbour's rough ground for about sixty thousand from savings if the price is fair, and replaces old gates.
S0.feel: Calm and glad, like a good harvest in the barn.
S0.quote: My grandfather bought this land with sweat, and I'd like to hand it to Daniel the same way, not with a computer in the middle.
S0.fieldNote: Karl's whole frame is inheritance: from grandfather to father to him to Daniel. His faith shows in how he speaks, 'thankful in the church sense'. He'd use savings to buy more land, a traditional way to invest. He tolerates his son's small modern touches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say every so often the world goes mad for something, and good farmers keep their heads down and wait. I'd say it at the livestock market. I'd also say the government shouldn't be throwing money at it, let the market sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I worry for Daniel more than for me. I've got ten years left. He's got forty, and he'll be farming against men with machines that never sleep. And he's more likely than me to want them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change anything myself in the first year. I'd tell Daniel that if he wants a robot, he can try one on hire, not buy one, and we'd see how it goes. I'd keep the savings where they are, in the building society and the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a cloud on the hill that might come this way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if Daniel wanted to borrow money for robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no, at first. We've never borrowed since my father paid off the bank in 1978. Then Margaret would say, Karl, it's his farm soon, and she'd be right, and I'd sulk for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would lose out in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young ones in the towns, I'd guess, the office ones. Out here, the farm's still there whatever happens. Land doesn't get made redundant.

S1.say: Every so often the world goes mad for something, and good farmers keep their heads down and wait. The government shouldn't throw money at it; let the market sort it.
S1.think: I worry for Daniel more than for me. I've got ten years left; he's got forty, farming against machines that never sleep.
S1.do: Changes nothing himself in the first year and keeps savings in the building society and land. Lets Daniel try a robot on hire rather than buy one.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a cloud on the hill that might come this way.
S1.quote: I've got ten years left. He's got forty, and he'll be farming against men with machines that never sleep.
S1.fieldNote: Karl's resistance meets his son's ambitions, and his wife is the one who tips the balance. The family hasn't borrowed since 1978, which he says with pride. He thinks land itself is safe even if people aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a much faster one, Karl. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what happens when governments let big companies run the country. I'd say it loudly at the market and to our MP if he showed his face. I wouldn't want handouts, I'd want them to stop it, or at least slow it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it'd scare me badly. Two years, and every big operator buys robots and sells beef cheaper than Daniel and I can. I could lose the farm my grandfather bought, not to a bank, but to a machine that doesn't even know what a Hereford is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sit down with Daniel and Margaret and work out how long we could run at a loss on our savings, maybe three or four years. I'd hand Daniel the running of the farm now, not in ten years, so he's the one deciding about machines. I'd talk to the minister at chapel about getting the farming families together, because we'd need each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at three walking the yard, and I've not done that since foot-and-mouth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't want handouts. What if the government offered support to farmers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it if it was for keeping farms going, like a grant for the farm. Not a cheque for sitting at home. There's a difference, and anyone who's farmed knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our Ellie's got two little ones, five and seven. I'd take them up the top field and show them where their great-great-grandfather's wall is. I'd want them to know this was ours, whatever happens to it.

S2.say: It's what happens when governments let big companies run the country. I don't want handouts; I want them to stop it, or at least slow it down.
S2.think: It'd scare me badly. I could lose the farm my grandfather bought, not to a bank but to a machine that doesn't know what a Hereford is.
S2.do: Works out with Daniel and Margaret that savings could carry three or four years of losses. Hands Daniel the running of the farm immediately and asks the chapel minister to bring farming families together.
S2.feel: Alarmed, walking the yard at three in the morning as he hasn't since foot-and-mouth.
S2.quote: I could lose the farm my grandfather bought, not to a bank, but to a machine that doesn't even know what a Hereford is.
S2.fieldNote: For Karl the two-year picture threatens the family line, not his income, and that is what alarms him. His response is family and faith community, not the state, and he draws a sharp line between farm support and 'a cheque for sitting at home'. Handing control to Daniel early is his biggest concession.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still too fast, but it's enough time for honest people to get ready. I'd tell the young farmers' club to learn the trade properly before they learn the machines. I'd say families should stick together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to sixty-three. I'd likely see the robots arrive from the kitchen window while Daniel goes out to meet them. It's not good, but it's not the end either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start handing the farm to Daniel over three years, on paper and in practice, with Margaret's accountant doing it properly. I'd keep our savings safe and pay down nothing, since we owe nothing. If Daniel wanted to try machines, I'd let him buy one, out of his share, and I'd keep my mouth shut. Mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I could plan, but I'd not like what I was planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Keeping your mouth shut sounds hard for you.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret laughed when I said that, didn't you hear her in the scullery? I'd manage it about half the time. The other half, Daniel would hear about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about five years that makes it better than two, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel gets to choose. In two years, the choice is made for him. In five, he's the farmer, and if he brings in robots, that's his decision. A man should run his own farm.

S3.say: Five years is still too fast, but enough time for honest people to get ready. Young farmers should learn the trade properly before the machines, and families should stick together.
S3.think: I'd likely see the robots arrive from the kitchen window while Daniel goes out to meet them. It's not good, but it's not the end.
S3.do: Hands the farm to Daniel over three years, formally and in practice, with the family accountant. Keeps savings safe and lets Daniel buy a machine from his own share without interfering, mostly.
S3.feel: Anxious; able to plan, but not liking the plan.
S3.quote: I'd likely see the robots arrive from the kitchen window while Daniel goes out to meet them.
S3.fieldNote: The main difference between two and five years for Karl is that his son gets to choose. 'A man should run his own farm' sums up his view. His wife's laugh from the next room showed she doubts he'll keep quiet about machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for anyone with any sense. Folk should get their families in order and get on with it. I'd still say the government should keep its nose out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years, I'll be sixty-eight and Daniel will be running it. If he's done it well, the farm survives. If he's borrowed too much for machines, it might not. That's the worry, not the robots themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd farm as normal for a few more years and hand over to Daniel around sixty-five. I'd encourage him to save up and buy machines when they're proven and cheap, not early. And I'd want our savings kept for a rainy day, not spent on gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. For Daniel, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What advice would you give Daniel, if he asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't borrow. My father said that to me, and I'll say it to him: a farm that owes nothing can't be taken. He'll not listen, but I'll say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything in that decade make you proud?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Daniel's lad, if he has one, wants to farm. Even with robots. As long as there's a Quinn on the land, I don't much mind what's in the shed.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty for anyone with sense. Folk should get their families in order and get on with it, and the government should keep its nose out.
S4.think: In ten years Daniel will be running it. If he's borrowed too much for machines, the farm might not survive, and that's my worry, not the robots.
S4.do: Farms as normal and hands over to Daniel around sixty-five. Encourages him to buy machines only when proven and cheap, and keeps the family savings for a rainy day.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but for his son rather than himself.
S4.quote: My father said that to me, and I'll say it to him: a farm that owes nothing can't be taken.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years removes Karl's personal stake and leaves only his fear of debt, passed down from his father. He would accept robots in the shed as long as there's a Quinn on the land. The phrase he repeats across scenarios is about not borrowing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. AGI by 2028. No time for Daniel to find his feet. What would help is the government slowing it down, and support for working farms to stay in families, not cheques for people to sit at home. And the chapel and neighbours pulling together, which they would.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A machine can do the hay, but it can't give thanks for it. Somebody has to stand at the gate and say, that was a good year.

headlineQuote: A machine can do the hay, but it can't give thanks for it. Somebody has to stand at the gate and say, that was a good year.
portrait: Karl Quinn, 58, farms the hundred and eighty acres his grandfather bought in 1951, with sixty Hereford cattle, two hundred ewes and traditional hay meadows, working alongside his son Daniel. He's a chapel-going traditionalist who distrusts government and big companies, never uses AI, and is proud that the family hasn't borrowed since 1978. Money isn't his worry; keeping the land in the family is. Two years of warning alarms him and makes him hand the farm to Daniel at once; five or ten let the handover happen properly, leaving only his fear that his son will borrow too much for machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time for his son Daniel to find his feet before the farm faced robot competition.
whatWouldHelp: The government slowing it down, support for working family farms rather than payments to sit at home, and the chapel and neighbours pulling together.
